client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away last month. Every time I try to sit down and focus on work, these memories of her just flood in and I can't concentrate on anything. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help, honestly — it feels like nothing can really fix the fact that she's just gone.
therapist: I'm so sorry for the loss of your grandmother — grief like this can make even ordinary tasks feel impossible, and what you're experiencing makes complete sense. You're right that nothing can "fix" her being gone, and I want you to know I'm not here to try to do that. I'm wondering, though, what would feel most meaningful to you right now — not fixing, but just having a space where she, and your pain, can be witnessed?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess... it does help a little to hear that you're not trying to make it all better, because that's what most people try to do and it just makes me feel more alone. Like they can't handle my sadness so they rush to fix it. I don't really know what "being witnessed" means for me, though — I'm not sure I even know how to talk about her without just falling apart.
therapist: What you just said about people rushing to fix your sadness — that's such a real and painful experience, feeling like your grief is too much for others to simply sit with. And I notice there's something tender in the way you're speaking right now, almost like you're holding yourself very carefully, which makes complete sense when you're afraid of falling apart. What if falling apart a little here was actually okay — what do you imagine might come out if you let yourself just say one small thing about her?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: She used to call me every Sunday morning, just to check in, and I'd sometimes let it go to voicemail because I was busy or just didn't feel like talking. And now I'd give anything to hear her voice again and I can't stop thinking about all those times I didn't pick up. I guess what comes out is mostly just... guilt, more than anything else.
therapist: That guilt you're describing is one of the most common and painful parts of grief — and it makes sense your mind keeps returning there. But I'm noticing something as you share this: your words carry so much weight, yet there's a quietness, almost a stillness, in the way you're saying it — like part of you has gone somewhere very still and far away. I'm curious, underneath that guilt, is there also something else — maybe sadness, or longing, or even love — that's harder to name?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah, I think there's a lot of love there, but it almost feels dangerous to go toward that because the love and the guilt are all tangled up together. Like if I let myself feel how much I loved her, it just makes the guilt worse — because why didn't I show it more when she was here. I don't know how you separate those things out, or if you even can.
therapist: What you're describing — love and guilt being tangled together — is actually something many people experience in grief, and it doesn't mean the love was insufficient, it means it was real. I'm struck by how softly and carefully you're speaking about this, like you're handling something very fragile, which tells me how much this love still matters to you. I wonder if it might be worth gently considering: do you think your grandmother experienced your love only through the calls you answered, or might she have held a fuller picture of you than the one your guilt is showing you right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I want to believe that, I really do, but my brain just keeps going back to the evidence against it — like all those missed calls feel so concrete and real, while the idea that she knew I loved her feels more like something I'm just telling myself to feel better. I know logically she probably did know, she never seemed upset with me or anything, but guilt doesn't really operate on logic, does it. It's like even when you make a good point, there's this part of me that just dismisses it and goes right back to the worst version of the story.
therapist: You've just named something really important — that guilt has its own logic, and it's very good at dismissing the evidence that doesn't fit the story it wants to tell. What you're describing is actually a pattern we can work with: your mind is selectively collecting the "proof" of failure while discounting the much larger body of evidence of your love. I'm curious — if a close friend came to you carrying this exact guilt about their grandmother, would you let them only count the missed calls, or would you help them see the whole picture?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I know the "talk to yourself like a friend" thing is supposed to help, and I can see why it makes sense, but honestly when I try to apply it to myself it just feels hollow — like I'm going through the motions of self-compassion without actually feeling it. I would absolutely tell a friend that a few missed calls don't erase a lifetime of love, but when it's me, it's like there's a different set of rules that I can't seem to override. I guess I don't really understand how you get from intellectually knowing something to actually feeling it in your gut.
therapist: What you're pointing to is one of the most honest things someone can say in this kind of work — that knowing and *feeling* are two very different things, and that gap can be really frustrating. I notice you're speaking quite quickly right now, like there's a lot rushing through you, and I wonder if part of that is a kind of urgency to *get there*, to close that gap — which itself might be worth slowing down around. The shift from head to gut usually doesn't come from trying harder to believe something, but from having experiences, even small ones, that slowly accumulate into a new felt sense — so I'm curious, are there any moments, even brief ones, where you *have* felt your love for her without the guilt immediately crowding in?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: Actually, yeah — there are these brief moments sometimes, usually when something random reminds me of her, like when I smell a certain kind of soap or hear an old song she liked. For just a second before my brain catches up, I feel this pure warmth, like she's just... present somehow, and it doesn't hurt yet. But then the guilt rushes in almost immediately and kind of contaminates it, and I feel almost guilty for even having that warm feeling, like I don't deserve it.
therapist: Those moments with the soap or the song — that pure warmth before your brain catches up — that *is* the love, unfiltered, and it's significant that it's still there and still comes to you. I want to gently push back on one thing: what if that warm feeling isn't something you have to deserve, but something she's actually still giving you? It might be worth holding onto those moments not as something to feel guilty about, but as small pieces of evidence that the connection between you two wasn't defined by a few missed calls.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: That reframe of it being something she's giving me rather than something I have to earn... that actually landed differently than I expected, and I'm not entirely sure why. But I'm also a little scared of leaning into it too much, because what if I start letting myself have those warm moments and then the guilt just hits harder afterward — like I've let my guard down. I don't know how to hold onto something tender without bracing for it to be taken away.
therapist: What you just described — bracing for something tender to be taken away — sounds like it might be bigger than just grief, like this is a pattern your heart has learned somewhere along the way to protect itself. That fear makes complete sense, and I don't want to rush past it, because learning to hold something precious without immediately armoring against losing it is actually some of the deepest work there is. I'm wondering, does that feeling of needing to brace yourself — does it show up in other places in your life, or does it feel particular to this loss?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: It definitely shows up in other places — I think I do it with friendships too, like I hold people at a slight distance because some part of me is always waiting for them to leave or get tired of me. I hadn't really connected that to my grandmother before, but maybe that's part of why the missed calls bother me so much — like I was already keeping her a little at arm's length without realizing it. It's uncomfortable to see that about myself, honestly.
therapist: The fact that you can see that about yourself — and say it out loud — takes real courage, and it's actually a profound moment of self-awareness rather than something to judge yourself for. What strikes me is that the distance you kept wasn't a failure of love; it sounds like it was a way of protecting yourself from the very pain you're feeling now, which means some part of you always knew how much she mattered. I'm curious — now that you've made that connection, does it shift anything in how you're understanding the missed calls?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: It does shift something, a little — like maybe the missed calls weren't me being a bad granddaughter but just me doing what I've always done with people I love, which is keep a small exit ready just in case. That actually makes me feel sad in a different way, less like I failed her and more like I wish I'd understood this about myself sooner, when there was still time to do something differently. I'm not sure that's better exactly, but it feels more true somehow.
therapist: What you just found — that this was a pattern, not a personal failing toward her — is a meaningful shift, and the sadness you're describing now sounds like grief with more room to breathe in it. There's something quietly significant in the way you said "more true somehow," because truth, even when it's sad, tends to feel more solid to stand on than guilt does. And that wish that you'd known this sooner — I want to hold that gently with you, because understanding it *now* still matters, and it can still change how you move toward the people you love.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech
